group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 35-year-old man, previously healthy enough to jog five kilometres three times a week but known to carry stage 3 chronic kidney disease attributed to childhood vesicoureteral reflux and a history of classical Hodgkin lymphoma that completed ABVD chemotherapy and mediastinal radiation five years earlier, came to the emergency department in late evening after forty-eight hours of escalating cough. He describes the illness as beginning with rhinorrhea and myalgias during a business flight, progressing the next morning to a persistent dry cough that became productive of rust-tinged sputum by lunchtime today, accompanied by mild chills, frontal pressure when bending forward, and a sense that deep breaths “catch” under the right costal margin. No vomiting, abdominal pain, dysuria, rash, or recent travel beyond the domestic flight is reported, and he denies cigarette or e-cigarette use, drinks beer only on weekends, and has never used recreational drugs. He lives with his partner in a downtown apartment, manages his own activities of daily living, and has not required hospitalisation since his oncology treatment concluded; follow-up imaging last autumn showed no evidence of recurrent malignancy. Outpatient laboratory monitoring two months ago documented a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL with a baseline blood urea nitrogen in the mid-teens, stable haemoglobin, and electrolytes within reference limits except for a tendency toward high-normal sodium felt to reflect his habit of vigorous exercise in a warm climate. Medications at home include lisinopril 10 mg each morning for renoprotective benefit, cholecalciferol 1000 IU daily, and an as-needed albuterol metered-dose inhaler that he last used a year ago for an upper-respiratory infection; he takes no diuretics, steroids, or anticoagulants. Vaccinations are up to date, including the most recent inactivated influenza dose administered at the workplace clinic in October. Review of systems is otherwise notable only for fatigue and decreased exercise tolerance—he could normally climb four flights of stairs without pausing but found himself winded halfway up one flight this afternoon. On arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, speaking in full sentences without audible wheeze, alert, and answering questions appropriately; he correctly stated the date, location, and situation. Triage vital signs obtained before any antipyretics, intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, or antibiotics revealed an oral temperature of 37.5 °C, heart rate 98 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 117/74 mm Hg in the right arm, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute with symmetrical chest expansion, and pulse oximetry 95 % while breathing ambient air at sea level. Physical examination demonstrated moist mucous membranes, no scleral icterus, a supple neck without jugular venous distension, and normal capillary refill. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a brisk rate consistent with the pulse but no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Pulmonary evaluation revealed slightly diminished breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right mid-posterior lung field, with dullness to percussion in the same region and preserved resonance elsewhere; no egophony was elicited over the spine, and there were no pleural rubs. Abdomen was soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds and no organomegaly. Extremities were warm without oedema or clubbing, and neurologic screening showed intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all limbs, symmetric reflexes, and a steady finger-to-nose test. Point-of-care capillary glucose measured 90 mg/dL. Venous and arterial blood specimens were drawn before therapy. Basic metabolic profile returned sodium 148 mEq/L, potassium 4.3 mEq/L, chloride 107 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.7 mg/dL, matching his recent baseline. Complete blood count showed a haematocrit of 52 %, leukocytes 12.1 × 10⁹/L with 80 % neutrophils, and platelets 280 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas obtained on room air displayed pH 7.48, PaCO₂ 33 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 90 mm Hg, consistent with a primary respiratory alkalosis likely driven by discomfort-related hyperventilation, without hypoxaemia. Lactate measured 1.3 mmol/L. A postero-anterior and lateral chest radiograph demonstrated a dense consolidation involving the right middle lobe with air bronchograms and preservation of the costophrenic angles; heart size was normal, mediastinum midline, and diaphragmatic contours were sharp. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 96–100 beats per minute without ischemic changes or conduction delay. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, urinary antigen tests for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a respiratory viral panel were dispatched to the laboratory, and no pharmacologic or supportive measures beyond routine blood sampling had been initiated at the time this examination was completed.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: a 35-year-old man starts at 35 points. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: stage 3 chronic kidney disease adds 10. Counting the Hodgkin lymphoma history as neoplastic disease adds 30. No liver disease, heart failure, or cerebrovascular disease is reported (0 each).
- Examination: alert, respiratory rate 14 (<30/min), systolic pressure 117 (≥90 mm Hg), temperature 37.5 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 98 (<125/min): 0 each.
- Tests: pH 7.48 (not <7.35), BUN 15 (not ≥30 mg/dL), sodium 148 (not <130 mEq/L), glucose 90 (not ≥250 mg/dL), hematocrit 52% (not <30%), and room-air PaO₂ 90 (not <60 mm Hg): 0 each. No pleural effusion: 0.
The result hinges on the cancer definition: the usual PSI definition requires active cancer or diagnosis within the past year, which would exclude this five-year remission and give 45. With lymphoma history counted, the sum is 35 + 10 + 30 + 0 + 0 = 75.
Final answer: 75
